newsitem.title: UK: Blair's speech wins over most British newspapers.
newsitem.headline: Blair's speech wins over most British newspapers.

text.p: Opposition leader Tony Blair won almost unalloyed approval from British newspapers on Wednesday for the powerful speech he gave to his Labour Party's last annual conference before a general election.

Most coveted of all, Blair commanded the support of the best-selling Sun tabloid newspaper, which in 1992 claimed its attacks on Labour had brought the Conservatives back to power for a fourth term of office.

"This was more than just a brilliant conference speech with something for everyone. It was a personal manifesto delivered with conviction by a man of decency and courage," said the Sun in an editorial.
"Now you must decide whether to give him your trust," the tabloid told its readers.

Blair made an impassioned address on Tuesday in which he sought to win over an electorate that last returned a Labour government 22 years ago. At the same time he tried to placate traditional socialists hostile to his radical bid to modernise the party.

He pledged to improve education and the skills of the British workforce, to halve youth unemployment, make the public sector more efficient and forge a more constructive relationship with the European Union.
He spelled out a "performance contract", inviting the nation to judge him on it after Labour's first five-year term. The general election must be held by next May.

"Yesterday, Mr Blair pointed the way to the future. Given the state of the Tory (Conservative) Party today, it cannot come a moment too soon," said the left-leaning Guardian. The Independent said that while Blair had overcome the conservative elements in his party, he had not yet shown whether he was capable of taking on contemporary vested interests. But, "if his manifesto is as it was presented yesterday -- radicalism rooted in the instincts of the middle class majority -- then it is, we suspect, a winning one," said the Independent's editorial.
The Times said Blair "spins words like spells and makes the future seem as though it is happening now".
But it warned against the kind of triumphalism that helped defeat Blair's predecessor, Neil Kinnock, at the 1992 election after opinion polls had shown Labour almost certain of victory.
"For every floating voter who responds to the ambition there will be another who recoils from the hubris," said the Times.
The only seriously hostile review came from the Conservative-supporting Daily Telegraph, which called the speech "presumptuous" and "in bad taste".
"Mr Blair...preaches away like a cross between an evangelical clergyman and an American management guru," said the Telegraph.
The ruling Conservatives, lagging Labour by around 20 points in opinion polls, also slammed the speech.
"This was one of the most deceitful speeches in British political history. Not a contract with Britain, but a con-trick on Britain," said deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine.
